The concept of the smartphone is approaching peak ergonomic refinement and thus peak minimalism. It's also approaching peak market saturation. So what can you really do with it in terms of design to distinguish or improve on any particular product? Round or flat edges? Choice of edge and backing materials? A choice of a few ports and buttons, or none at all? That's all cosmetic. There's little left that you might do in terms of physical design that has any significance to the user experience. The most radical things on the horizon in that context are flexibility (which will likely prove pointless save for making phones more child/idiot-proof), solar screens, gesture sensing, wireless charging, and wireless connectivity. A totally wireless hermetically sealed smartphone is probably just a year or two away, and that will be the period at the end of the smartphone design evolution story. Practical features are really all down to numbers now. Screen dimensions. Screen resolution. Thinness. (which will probably bottom-out at around 4mm--the thickness of a clipboard--for all these devices within a few years) Weight. Memory capacity. Processor performance. Battery life. Camera performance statistics. Computing hardware in general is on a long-term trend of commodification and virtuallization. Physical design for all these devices is becoming irrelevant.

So the most radical innovations a company like Apple, or any of its competitors, could try is to explore completely new paradigms in mobile communications if they can imagine them--which, of course, we've seen them trying with smartwatches. For instance, abandoning the Swiss Army Knife paradigm of the smartphone in favor of sets of more specialized devices that are ergonomically superior. Or trying some bleeding-edge technology like sub-vocal speech recognition for silent telepathy-like telephony and the use of all-audio agent-based user interfaces, thus reducing the smartphone to a headset. Really, now that we have Siri and Cortana, screens are redundant for a lot of the uses of smartphones. For just making calls, you could readily reduce things to a device like Samsung's pen-like Bluetooth handset driven by voice alone.

The term smart 'phone' is beginning to become silly. Actual telephony use is in decline across the collective applications of these devices. People who actually need a phone to use routinely prefer lower-tech cell phones. The concept of a 'phone company' as a business model is itself anachronistic. We should really be calling these pocket PADs or the like.

I was born in 1960 and grew up watching (and loving!) old reruns of Leave it to Beaver. There was one episode where Beaver (the younger naive little brother -- the titular star of the show) was being schooled by an older kid who had just moved into Beaver's neighborhood. This older kid spoke Spanish and this piqued Beaver's curiosity. So Beaver asked this kid to teach him how to say something in Spanish.

The kid taught him the phrase (and I still remember it to this day because I memorized it along with Beaver) "Usted tiene una cara como puerco." and told Beaver to go up to this fat girl and say that to her. Beaver asked him what it meant and the kid lied and said it was a compliment. So Beaver goes up to the girl and says it and everyone sniggers and the fat girl runs away in tears. (I guess she understood Spanish too.)

When Beaver asked the kid why the girl ran away crying, he burst out laughing and said, "You just told her she has a face like a pig!". I thought it was hilarious and couldn't wait to use this cool new phrase on someone in my life. So I became that older mean kid and waited until Thanksgiving a few weeks later, when our Aunt made her annual pilgrimage to our house with her kids (my three cousins).

The youngest of those three cousins was a girl who had two older brothers. I was nine years old and she was five. At one point during her visit, I called her aside and told her I learned a cool new phrase in Spanish and I was going to teach it to her and she could go up to her Mom and say it and everyone would think she is cool too for speaking Spanish.

I should probably mention at this point that my Aunt was a fucking PLANET, especially for those times (this was 1969). At that point in my young life, she was the ONLY fat person I had ever seen in person and I used to gawk at her when she visited. She kind of scared me, even, because it was mind-boggling to me how a single person could be so gargantuan. I felt kind of sorry for my cousins because I figured they were embarrassed by their mother -- I know it would have mortified me if my own mother showed up at school events looking like a swollen pig. But I was also an asshole and all I cared about was re-creating that delicious scene I had watched on TV. When my cousin asked what it meant I told her it meant her mother was pretty. Teehee.

Finally after I insisted that my cousin rehearse the sentence over and over and I figured she was as close to getting it right as she was going to be, the big moment came. The plan was that she was going to venture upstairs where the grownups were sitting around the table talking, approach her mother, and show off her newfound Spanish abilities.

Needless to say, chaos ensued. The rest of us cousins were gathered at the bottom of the stairs, straining to hear it go down. We heard the adults talking, then silence, then, "What?!! What are you trying to say?" from my Aunt. A brief silence again while my cousin apparently repeated herself, then... "Reeeeeeeee! Who taught you that?! That is very rude and don't you ever say that again! Reeeeeeeee!" Little cousin is now thoroughly confused and in trouble so she comes running back downstairs.

I grabbed her and said, "Did you tell them who taught you?" and she said, "No! They got mad!".

My (human-sized) mother came storming downstairs next. "What are you all doing down here?!" she bellowed. Knowing my mother's temper, I kept a low profile and no one else said anything either. She wasn't really in the mood to get to the bottom of it so she just said, "Knock it off and stop being so mean!", then thankfully she left to rejoin the other adults.

It was a close call and to this day when I look back on that event I am still amused at how my natural shitlady tendencies have been around from an early age... I just didn't know what it was called yet or how important it was going to be some day to continue my shitlady ways because by 2016 hams like my memorable Aunt are a dime a dozen. Good times...
